passage: "You said you'd call my parents back. You said it on Tuesday. Do you even care about meeting them, Kaito?" Sami was standing by the counter of their small Toronto apartment, still wearing her work lanyard. Kaito felt the words land one after another like hail. His chest tightened; his mind went blank. He heard himself say, "Can we not do this now," and then he reached for his earphones and turned to the laptop. In his head he was being sensible: no shouting, no fight. Behind him, Sami's voice went up, then stopped. He didn't turn around. He didn't see her sit down on the floor by the counter, staring at the back of his head, feeling more alone than if he had left the room.

qa.q: What had Kaito said he would do?
qa.a: He said he'd call Sami's parents back.

qa.q: What did Kaito think he was doing when he put on his earphones?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed, with his chest tight and his mind blank, and thought he was being sensible by avoiding a fight.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Kaito at this stage?
qa.a: He could say "I'm overwhelmed, give me twenty minutes and I'll come back to this" instead of turning away in silence.

qa.q: How does Sami experience Kaito turning to his laptop?
qa.a: She feels abandoned; sitting on the floor staring at his back, she feels more alone than if he had left the room.

grounding: Shows a young man hearing criticism, feeling overwhelmed and retreating behind earphones, while his partner experiences it as abandonment.

passage: The college library closed at nine, and Usha caught Imran by the photocopier at ten to. "You've skipped dinner with me three times this week. You don't reply for hours. What am I supposed to think?" Two juniors looked up from the reading table. Imran's ears went hot. Every sentence felt like a list of his failures being read aloud. He picked up his copies, said, "I've got a deadline," and walked to the stairs. In his head he was protecting them both from a scene in the library. Usha stood by the machine, still holding the question she hadn't finished. The librarian was switching off the lights row by row, and to her it felt as if he had switched her off too.

qa.q: Where did Usha catch Imran?
qa.a: She caught Imran by the photocopier.

qa.q: Why did Imran walk away to the stairs?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and exposed, as if a list of his failures was being read aloud in front of the juniors, and believed leaving would protect them both from a scene.

qa.q: What could Imran say instead of walking off?
qa.a: He could say "I'm swamped right now, can we talk after the library closes?" so Usha knows he is coming back.

qa.q: What is it like for Usha as the lights go off?
qa.a: Usha feels switched off and left behind, still holding an unfinished question, as if Imran had shut her out.

grounding: Shows a student flooded by his partner's criticism who walks away to avoid a scene, while she experiences it as being abandoned.

passage:
Bhupen had barely parked the tractor behind the mill when Nazia came out of the kitchen, her dupatta tight around her fist. "You said you'd be back by four. You said you'd talk to Abba about our house. You say a lot of things."
The list kept coming. His chest went tight, his ears buzzed, and the words blurred into one long noise. He couldn't find a single sentence to answer.
So he said nothing. He took the bucket and walked down to the well, slowly, not looking back.
In his head he was being sensible: no shouting, no fight. Behind him, Nazia stood in the doorway, watching his back get smaller, and felt like she'd been left standing alone in a field.

qa.q: Where did Bhupen go when Nazia was talking?
qa.a: He took the bucket and walked down to the well.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling as the list of complaints kept coming?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and flooded; his chest went tight, his ears buzzed and he couldn't find a sentence to answer.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Bhupen at this stage?
qa.a: He could say something short like "I'm overwhelmed, give me ten minutes and I'll come back," so his silence doesn't feel like leaving.

qa.q: How does Nazia experience Bhupen walking away?
qa.a: She feels abandoned and alone, as if she has been left standing in a field, even though he thinks he is avoiding a fight.

grounding: A young man hears his wife's complaints, feels flooded and walks away silently, thinking he is avoiding a fight while she feels abandoned.

passage:
Anders came back from his lecture in Uppsala to find Dalia sitting on his bed with her laptop closed. "We need to talk. You haven't asked me one thing about my week. You didn't come to my concert. Do you even want this?"
Her voice rose on each question. Anders felt his head fill with static. Every word sounded like proof he was failing.
He didn't argue. He pulled his earphones out of his pocket, put them in, and started unpacking his books.
"Seriously?" said Dalia.
He thought he was being kind by not snapping at her. Dalia sat very still, and then she picked up her coat and left, feeling like she had just been shut out of the room.

qa.q: What did Anders do with his earphones?
qa.a: He pulled them out of his pocket, put them in and started unpacking his books.

qa.q: What was Anders feeling as Dalia's questions came?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and like a failure; his head filled with static and every word sounded like proof he was failing.

qa.q: What could help at this stage instead of the earphones?
qa.a: Anders could tell Dalia he is overwhelmed and needs a short break, and give a time to come back, so she doesn't feel shut out.

qa.q: How does Dalia experience the earphones?
qa.a: She feels shut out and abandoned, as if he chose silence over her, which is why she left.

grounding: A young man feels flooded by criticism and puts in his earphones to avoid a fight, while his partner experiences it as being abandoned.

passage:
In the break room of the call centre, Zainab had waited forty minutes for Hrithik's shift to end. "You didn't reply all day. You forgot my interview. Why do I always have to chase you?"
Two colleagues looked up from their tea. Hrithik felt his face go hot and his mind go blank. He could hear his manager's voice from earlier, still telling him he was too slow. Now this.
"I need to go," he mumbled, and walked out to the parking lot without his lunch box.
He told himself it was better than fighting in front of people. Zainab stood by the vending machine, holding the lunch box he'd left, feeling as if he'd simply switched her off.

qa.q: How long had Zainab waited for Hrithik's shift to end?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when Zainab confronted him in the break room?
qa.a: He felt flooded and ashamed; his face went hot and his mind went blank, especially after his manager's criticism earlier.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Hrithik here?
qa.a: He could tell Zainab he's overwhelmed and ask to talk after a short break outside, naming when he'll come back instead of just leaving.

qa.q: How does Zainab experience Hrithik walking out?
qa.a: She feels abandoned and switched off, holding his forgotten lunch box, even though he believes he is avoiding a public fight.

grounding: A young man, already criticised at work, feels flooded by his partner's complaints and leaves, while she experiences it as being abandoned.

passage:
Dilnaz,

You asked me last night, crying, why I always "disappear." I couldn't answer then. I'm trying now, on paper, where my voice doesn't lock up.

When you start with "we need to talk" and then "you never" and "why don't you," something in my chest goes tight and loud, like a pressure cooker. I can't find words fast enough. Anything I say feels like it'll make it worse. So I go quiet. I put my earphones in. Yesterday I walked out and sat on the hostel terrace for an hour.

In my head, I'm stopping a fight. I honestly thought I was protecting us.

But I saw your face when I came back. You looked like I'd left you at a station. I didn't know it felt like that for you.

I don't know how to fix it yet. I just didn't want you to think I don't care.

Danish

qa.q: Where did Danish sit for an hour after walking out?
qa.a: Danish sat on the hostel terrace for an hour.

qa.q: What does Danish feel when Dilnaz starts with 'we need to talk'?
qa.a: Danish feels overwhelmed, a tight, loud pressure in the chest, and can't find words, so going quiet feels like the only safe option.

qa.q: What could Danish try instead of putting in earphones or leaving?
qa.a: Danish could say, 'I'm overwhelmed, give me a little time and I'll come back to this,' so the pause doesn't feel like abandonment.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz experience Danish going quiet?
qa.a: Dilnaz feels abandoned and hurt, as if left at a station, rather than seeing it as avoiding a fight.

grounding: A letter shows one partner flooding under criticism and withdrawing to avoid a fight, while the other experiences it as abandonment.
